::: {.callout-tip}
#### Learning Objectives

- Understand why log transformation is not needed when preparing data for
  spatial proteomics, unlike expression proteomics
- Understand the different role normalisation plays in spatial proteomics,
  and be able to apply row-sum normalisation with `normalize()`
- Be able to aggregate precursor-level data to protein level with
  `aggregateFeatures()`, and understand how the choice of aggregation
  function relates to the scale of the data
- Know how to concatenate replicates into a single dataset with
  `joinAssays()` and keep only proteins found in all replicates
- Summarise peptide support (the number of precursors per protein) and the
  proportion of imputed values per protein, and add them to the joined data
- Understand the benefits and limitations of concatenating datasets for
  downstream machine learning
:::


```{r}
#| label: load-dia-data-filtered
#| include: false

library("here")
library("QFeatures")
library("tidyr")
library("dplyr")
library("ggplot2")
library("patchwork")
library("stringr")

load(here("course_files/preprocessed/P1_lesson04.rda"), verbose = TRUE)
```

In our previous expression proteomics workflow we described the processing steps
required to prepare quantitative proteomics data for differential abundance 
analysis [@Hutchings2023]. Such preparation involved log2 transformation of the
peptide-level quantitation data before aggregating to the protein level and 
normalising. These steps differ from those required when processing subcellular
spatial proteomics data.

Quantitative proteomics data often undergoes logarithmic transformation prior to
statistical analysis. The reason for this is that the majority of statistical
tests require the data to display a normal distribution. Whilst raw quantitative
MS-based proteomics data is dramatically skewed towards 0, the log2 transformed 
data is approximately normal. In this subcellular spatial proteomics workflow,
however, the goal is not to prepare our data for downstream statistical differential 
abundance analysis. Instead, we are preparing the data for a machine learning
classifier for which the input is protein correlation profiles across a
biochemical gradient. The machine learning algorithm which we will use does 
not make the assumption that our data has a normal distribution, therefore we
do not need to perform logarithmic transformation. In fact, logarithmic
transformation would reduce the subcellular resolution by flattening our abundance
distribution profiles. 

The second data processing step which differs between expression and spatial 
proteomics analysis is that of normalisation. In most proteomics experiments the
goal of normalisation is to remove any technological variation and account for 
experimental error. As a result, normalised data should contain near-identical
samples in which the majority of variation is of biological importance. In spatial
proteomics normalisation plays a different role because we are interested in the
shape of protein abundance profiles rather than the magnitude of the intensity in
each channel. Hence, the aim of normalisation here is to scale all of our
quantitation data into the same space (within the range of 0 and 1) whilst 
maintaining the shape of our abundance profiles. If we did not do this, proteins
with the same distribution across the gradient but different abundances would 
display very different profiles.


## Normalisation 

Based on De Duve's principle [@deDuve1964] we know that proteins which are
co-localised within the cell will exhibit similar abundance distribution profiles
across a fractionation gradient. This means that we we can infer the location of 
proteins by matching their abundance profiles to profiles of well-known organelle 
residents, termed "markers". In order to get information about the abundance
distribution of each protein across the fractionation gradient we need to carry 
out row sum normalisation. To do this we make use of the `normalize` function 
within the `QFeatures` infrastructure. 

```{r}
# Define number of replicates
R <- 1:3
```


```{r}
## Define names for indexing imputed datasets
imp_names <- paste0("imp_precursors_R", R)

## Define new names for normalised datasets
norm_names <- paste0("norm_precursors_R", R)

qf <- normalize(qf, 
                i = imp_names,
                name = norm_names,
                method = "sum")

qf
```

Let's take a look at what this normalisation has done to the data.

```{r}
## Before normalisation
qf[["imp_precursors_R1"]] |>
  assay() |>
  head()

## After normalisation
qf[["norm_precursors_R1"]] |>
  assay() |>
  head()
```

Through the process of row sum normalisation we have now converted our raw
quantitative values into a *correlation profile* or *protein profile* across the
fractionation gradient. The abundance values represent the proportion of total
quantification for each precursor that comes from each fraction, with each row
sum being equal to 1. This scales all data into the same space so that we can
use the shape rather than the intensity of profiles for downstream machine
learning.


```{r, fig.height=5}
plot(qf)
```

Let's take a look at what normalisation has done to the data, starting with 
replicate 1. 

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
## Evaluate the effect of data normalisation on rep1

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

## Plot pre-normalised data
qf[["imp_precursors_R1"]] |>
  assay() |>
  longForm() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = colname, y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "", y = "Raw abundance", title = "Pre-normalisation") +
  theme_bw()

## Plot post-normalised data
qf[["norm_precursors_R1"]] |>
  assay() |>
  longForm() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = colname, y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "", y = "Normalised abundance", title = "Post-normalisation") +
  theme_bw()
```

We can see from these plots that the raw precursor abundance values are spread 
across a wide dynamic range, spanning 7 orders of magnitude. This is very normal
for cellular proteomics data. If we were to use the pre-normalised data, the 
profile of a high abundance protein would be numerically very different to that
of a low abundance protein, even if they fractionate in the same pattern across
our biochemical gradient. Once we normalise our precursors, all have an abundance
between 0 and 1. We can now see some shape to the profiles.

Unlike in total proteome experiments where normalisation aims to remove variation,
we do not expect the boxplots of normalised correlation profiles to be perfectly
aligned. For each fraction, many proteins have low to 0 abundance. These are
proteins that belong to organelles that primarily sediment elsewhere in the
gradient. However, each fraction also has a long tail towards 1, indicating a 
subset of proteins that did predominantly pellet in this fraction. A box plot with
shape and structure like this is a first indication that our experiment may have
worked - we would not want a flat profile of boxplots.

::: {.callout-note}
#### At what stage should I normalise to generate profiles?

#### Before or after imputation? (Depends on extent of data missingness)

Some experimental designs yield a relatively low proportion of missing values,
for example label-based methods that use TMT such as LOPIT. As a result, after
an initial filtering step, there are very few values to impute. Applying a
baseline k-NN imputation to such data can be more successful when the data are in a
similar space after normalisation, as discussed in @Hutchings2025. We note that by applying
imputation after normalisation, the final imputed profiles will no longer sum to
exactly 1. However, since such designs have such low missingness, the sum should
not greatly exceed 1. By contrast, where datasets have a greater proportion of
missing data to impute, as is the case for this example where we have a DIA LFQ
design row sum normalisation of a limited number of fractions would generate a
short profile summed to one and subsequent imputation could result in a
correlation profile with an undesirably high sum value. Here it is necessary to
impute prior to normalisation to ensure the generation of sensible correlation
profiles in the same final space (between 0 and 1).

#### Before or after aggregation? (In practice, it makes little difference)

In this workflow we normalise each precursor profile to sum to 1 *before*
aggregating to protein level. Precursors from the same protein can differ in
raw intensity by orders of magnitude, mainly because they ionise differently,
not because of the biology. If we aggregated raw intensities, a single very
intense precursor could largely determine the protein's profile.

For localisation, what matters is the *shape* of the profile across
fractions, and each precursor is an independent measurement of that shape.
Normalising first puts all precursors on the same scale, so each contributes
equally to the protein profile. Aggregating with a median then gives a
consensus profile that is robust to the occasional precursor with an
unusual profile.

The trade-off is that low-intensity, noisier precursors are given the same
weight as high-intensity ones. Our earlier intensity-based filtering helps
by removing the weakest precursors. Because the median of profiles that
each sum to 1 does not itself sum exactly to 1, we normalise once more
after aggregation.

In practice, we find the order makes little difference to the resolution of
the final spatial map. Either approach is reasonable, as long as the final
protein profiles are normalised before downstream analysis.
:::


## Aggregation

Now that we have our final precursor-level dataset we can aggregate this upward
to the protein level. The aim of this step is to combine data from all component
precursors into a single protein-level entry. This entry will have one master
protein accession and one quantitative value per biochemical fraction per
sample.

Within the `QFeatures` infrastructure aggregation is carried out using the
`aggregateFeatures` function. This function provides users with several options
on how to aggregate multiple quantitation values into a single value. The
methods differ with respect to how they deal with missing data as well as
whether they require log2 or raw quantitation data as their input.

In our sister workflow @Hutchings2023 we aggregate using `robustSummary`, a
state-of-the-art aggregation method which is notably robust to outliers and
missing values [@Sticker2020; @Goeminne2016]. However, our data is not currently
suitable for `robustSummary` aggregation as this method requires log2
transformed data. Whilst it would be relatively simple to log2 transform our
quantitative data using the `logTransform` function within the `QFeatures`
infrastructure, we would need to reverse this transformation by taking the
exponential of the resulting protein data, which is not so simple. Instead we
will aggregate precursors straight to protein level using `colMedians` method from the
`matrixStats` package. We specify this method using the `fun = ` argument, as
well as telling the function which `rowData` column we wish to use for
aggregation.

Here, we demonstrate one-step aggregation, from precursors directly to protein.
This means aggregating all precursors with the same value of `"Protein.Group"`.
For an example of two-step aggregation, from precursor to peptide followed by
peptide to protein, users are directed to @Hutchings2023.

```{r, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
agg_names <- paste0("proteins_R", R)

qf <- QFeatures::aggregateFeatures(qf,
                                   i = norm_names,
                                   fcol = "Protein.Group", 
                                   name = agg_names,
                                   fun = matrixStats::colMedians)
## Verify
qf
```

We have now populated the `QFeatures` object with protein-level data containing
the row normalised protein correlation profiles. From looking at the summary in 
`experiments(qf)` we have around 9000 proteins in each replicate experiment.
These protein correlation profiles contain spatial information and are the input
to downstream machine learning classifers.


```{r, fig.height=5}
plot(qf)
```


::: {.callout-exercise}
#### Challenge: Using the .n column from aggregateFeatures

{{< level 2 >}}

1. Look at the `??aggregateFeatures` help documentation. What is the `.n` column?
What does the column mean for our data specifically?

2. Plot a histogram to explore the `.n` column in replicate 1 of our aggregated
protein-level data. 


::::: {.callout-answer collapse="true"}

**Task 1**
\
One advantage of using the `aggregateFeatures` function is that it automatically
adds a column to the aggregated data to indicate how many lower-level features
(here precursors) were aggregated into each higher-level feature (here protein
groups). This column is called `.n`. Of note, this column is created every time
you use the `aggregateFeatures` function, and always has the same name. Hence, 
if you did a two-step aggregation from precursors to peptides to proteins, the
`.n` column in the peptide-level data would indicate how many precursors per peptide
and in the protein-level data would be how many peptides per protein. 


**Task 2**
\
Let's plot a histogram of the precursor support per protein group in our dataset.
Again, we demonstrate with replicate 1 but advise users to plot for all replicates
of all conditions.

```{r}
qf[["proteins_R1"]] |>
  rowData() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = `.n`)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  labs(x = "Precursor support", y = "Number of proteins") +
  theme_bw()
```

This initial histogram shows us that most proteins have < 100 precursors supporting
them, which is not surprising. It's hard to see how low with the current binning.
Let's create bins for 1-20 and then merge all others into a > 20 category.

```{r}
qf[["proteins_R1"]] |>
  rowData() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(n_binned = factor(
    if_else(.n > 20, ">20", as.character(.n)),
    levels = c(as.character(1:20), ">20"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n_binned)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Precursor support", y = "Number of proteins") +
  theme_bw()
```


:::::
:::


### Re-normalisation

Before aggregation, each precursor profile summed to 1. However, the median
of several profiles that each sum to 1 does not itself sum exactly to 1.
Let's check the row sums of our protein-level data.

```{r}
qf[["proteins_R1"]] |>
  assay() |>
  rowSums() |>
  summary()
```

The row sums are close to 1, but not exactly 1. To make sure every protein
profile is on exactly the same scale before machine learning, we apply
row-sum normalisation once more, this time at the protein level.

```{r}
prot_norm_names <- paste0("proteins_norm_R", R)

qf <- normalize(qf,
                i = agg_names,
                name = prot_norm_names,
                method = "sum")

qf
```

Every protein profile should now sum to exactly 1.

```{r}
qf[["proteins_norm_R1"]] |>
  assay() |>
  rowSums() |>
  summary()
```

This step changes the scale of each profile very slightly but does not change
its shape, so the spatial information is preserved.

## Concatenating datasets for machine learning

Previous subcellular proteomics experiments utilising protein correlation
profiles have benefited from the combining of datasets 
[@Barylyuk2020; @Christoforou2016; @Moloney2023], that is the concatenation of 
replicates or experiments that utilise different gradients [@Trotter2010]. Since
the use-case experiment included three biological replicates each with 9
biochemical fractions we can concatenate these data into a single dataset
with 27 columns. In order to do this, the column names must be different in each
replicate. By looking at the `colnames` of each experimental set per condition
we verify we indeed have unique names.

```{r}
colnames(qf[["proteins_R1"]])
colnames(qf[["proteins_R2"]])
colnames(qf[["proteins_R3"]])
```


If the `colnames` were not unique to each replicate we would have to use the
`renameColname` function, specifying which experimental set we wish to change
the column names of (`i = ` argument) and then providing a vector of new column
names (`value = ` argument).

We can use `joinAssays` to concatenate the fractions across replicates to
improve the discrimination between organelle signatures.

```{r concatenate_replicates}
agg_names <- c("proteins_norm_R1", 
               "proteins_norm_R2", 
               "proteins_norm_R3")

qf <- joinAssays(qf, 
                 i = agg_names, 
                 name = "proteins_joined")
## Verify
qf
```

Finally, we filter to only keep proteins that are found in all replicates. This
is necessary because the machine learning algorithms in `pRoloc` do not accept
missingness.

```{r}
qf <- filterNA(qf, i = "proteins_joined")

## Verify
qf
```

We see our final protein level data contain `r nrow(qf[["proteins_joined"]])`
proteins.

```{r, fig.height=5}
plot(qf)
```

### Concatenation gives equal weight to all replicates

By concatenating the datasets we give each biological replicate an equal weight 
for the downstream machine learning classification. This means that any variability
between experiments will be accounted for. For example, if a
protein has an abundance distribution profile similar to that of nuclear protein
markers in one of the three replicates, but is more similar to cytoplasmic markers
in the remaining two replicates, this will be reflected by the fact that the 
protein will either be classified with a lower confidence or not classified at
all. If each replicate was analysed separately, the protein may receive conflicting
classifications in each replicate which would require a user-defined resolution.

Another potential advantage of concatenating datasets is the inclusion of data
derived from different gradient variations [@Barylyuk2020; @Trotter2010]. Although
many subcellular compartments are well resolved using a single gradient, some 
compartments remain more challenging to resolve due to their similarities or
connections with other compartments. For example, compartments within the endomembrane
system can generate similar fractionation profiles. Where no single gradient will
provide optimal separation of all organelles of interest, it is possible to design
different gradients which provide optimal separation different organelles. These
data can then be concatenated to generated a combined dataset with greater final
resolution of all desired compartments. 

Overall, data concatenation has been shown to have benefits for downstream machine
learning in many cases. Ultimately, however, the decision to concatenate replicates 
will depend on the goal of the experiment and type of data analysis required to
answer the experimental question. In particular, where the experimental aim is to
identify differential localisation between conditions it is recommended to repeat
the same biochemical gradient across all three replicates to avoid complicating
downstream analysis.

### Keeping track of peptide support and missing values

Before we move on, we record two pieces of information about the quality of
each protein profile, so that we can use them later when interpreting our
spatial maps:

1. **Peptide support**: the number of precursors used to calculate each protein
   profile. Proteins quantified from only one or two precursors tend to have
   noisier profiles. `aggregateFeatures` recorded this in a `rowData` column
   called `.n`.
2. **Missing values**: how much of each profile was imputed. In the previous
   lesson we recorded the number of missing values per precursor, before
   imputation, in a `rowData` column called `nNA`. Proteins whose precursors
   had many missing values rely more heavily on imputation and should be
   interpreted with more caution.

Neither of these makes it through to the joined set. `aggregateFeatures` does
not carry `nNA` up to the protein level, and `joinAssays` only keeps `rowData`
columns that are identical in every set, which `.n` is not.

```{r}
## .n is in the protein-level set of each replicate...
rowData(qf[["proteins_R1"]])$.n |>
  summary()

## ...but not in the joined set
".n" %in% colnames(rowData(qf[["proteins_joined"]]))
```

We have written a small function, `addProfileQC()`, that summarises these to
the protein level for each replicate and adds them to the joined set. For
each protein it calculates the proportion of its precursor values that were
missing before imputation, and then adds the following columns to the joined
set:

* `n_rep1`, `n_rep2`, `n_rep3`: number of precursors in each replicate
* `n_min`, `n_mean`: minimum and mean across replicates
* `missing_rep1`, `missing_rep2`, `missing_rep3`: proportion of values missing
  before imputation in each replicate
* `missing_max`, `missing_mean`: maximum and mean across replicates

We report the minimum peptide support and maximum missingness because a
protein profile is only as good as its weakest replicate.

```{r, file = here("materials/code/add_profile_qc.R")}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the addProfileQC() function"
```

```{r, include=FALSE}
source(here("materials/code/add_profile_qc.R"))
```

```{r}
qf <- addProfileQC(qf,
                   prec_sets = c(rep1 = "norm_precursors_R1",
                                 rep2 = "norm_precursors_R2",
                                 rep3 = "norm_precursors_R3"),
                   prot_sets = c(rep1 = "proteins_R1",
                                 rep2 = "proteins_R2",
                                 rep3 = "proteins_R3"),
                   joined_set = "proteins_joined")

## Verify
rowData(qf[["proteins_joined"]]) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  dplyr::select(starts_with("n_"), starts_with("missing_")) |>
  head()
```

These columns will be carried over into part 2 of the course, where we will
use them to help interpret our spatial maps.



```{r}
#| label: create-protein-dataset
#| include: false

save(qf, file = here("course_files/preprocessed/P1_lesson05.rda"))
```


::: {.callout-tip}
#### Key Points

- Spatial proteomics data are prepared for machine learning on profile
  *shape*, not for statistical tests, so log transformation is not needed
  and would flatten the profiles.
- Row-sum normalisation turns raw intensities into profiles that sum to 1.
  This puts all features on the same scale while preserving the shape of
  their distribution across the gradient.
- For sparse label-free data, impute before normalising, so that profiles
  are complete before they are scaled.
- Aggregation combines precursors into one profile per protein group. The
  aggregation method must match the data: `robustSummary` needs
  log-transformed input, whereas `colMedians` can be used on normalised
  profiles directly.
- Whether you normalise before or after aggregation makes little practical
  difference, as long as the final protein profiles are normalised.
- `aggregateFeatures()` and `joinAssays()` only keep `rowData` columns that
  are the same for every feature being combined, so per-replicate quality
  information, such as the number of precursors (`.n`) and the proportion of
  missing values, must be summarised and added back to the joined set.
- Concatenating replicates with `joinAssays()` gives each replicate equal
  weight in classification, so inconsistent proteins are classified with
  lower confidence rather than given conflicting labels.
- Concatenation can also combine different gradients to improve resolution.
  For differential localisation between conditions, however, the same
  gradient should be used across all replicates.
:::
